title: The effect of seismic airgun surveys on leatherback sea turtles (Dermochelys coriacea) during the nesting season.
full_text:
# **The effect of seismic airgun surveys on leatherback sea turtles** _**(Dermochelys coriacea**_ **) during the nesting season.**

## **Final Report to BHP Petroleum (Trinidad) Ltd.**

Scott A. Eckert, Ph.D. Ann Bowles, Ph.D. Eric Berg Hubbs-Sea World Research Insititute San Diego, CA.  92109 USA

Tel. 619-226-3870; Fax. 619-226-3944; email seckert@hswri.org

## **Background**

The leatherback sea turtle, _Dermochelys coriacea_ is the oldest and largest of the marine turtles.  It is characterized by an exceptionally streamlined body form that does not have the hard shell found in all the other species, rather the turtle is entirely skin covered (Figure 1).  Distribution

Figure 1.  Leatherback sea turtles are the most well-adapted turtle for living in the open ocean.

ranges from 71 degrees north to 47 degrees south, but is generally considered temperate to north temperate.  The leatherback’s diet consists primarily of jellyfish or other jelly-like animals and may be one of the primary motivations for the species’ temperate distribution as these prey are  particularly abundant in colder waters.  The pelagic nature of this turtle has given it a large number of behavioral and physiological differences when compared to most other turtle species.  The leatherback is exceptionally active, and  while in the tropics they rarely cease swimming.  Swim speed averages .6 - .85 meters per second (2.16 km/hr - 3.06 km/hr), and they travel between 45 and 60 km per day (S. Eckert unpub. data).  Leatherbacks are also extremely good divers, regularly diving

beyond 100 meters in depth, with the record beyond 1000 meters (Eckert et al., 1996).  Dive durations average between 10 and 15 minutes (maximum = 42 minutes) and occur regularly throughout day and night (Eckert et al. 1986, 1989, 1996).  Physiologically they are quite different from other turtles in that they tend to minimize pulmonary oxygen stores in favor of tissue based stores such as is found in muscle and blood (in the form of elevated hemoglobin and myoglobin concentrations) (Eckert, 1989).  This means that the leatherback is generally a very aerobic and active animal, in contrast to most reptiles that tend to be active in bouts or periods.  However, it also means that the species is less well equipped to handle physiological stresses encountered during forced or extended submergence or other aquatic perturbations.

While leatherbacks are generally assumed to remain in cooler waters, gravid females migrate to tropical beaches to nest.  Once mature (after they are approximately 20 years old), each female will migrate thousands of kilometers to nest on the beach where she was hatched (Figure 2).  These migrations take place every two or three years, and the turtle will remain within 50 km of the nesting beach during that nesting season (Chan et al. 1990, Figure 2.  Leatherback sea turtle nesting. S.A. Eckert, 1997).  Each turtle will deposit

on average 6 - 7 nests (11 maximum) over the course of the 2-3 month season with each turtle nesting every 10 days (K.L. Eckert, 1987).  Nest incubation requires between 60 - 70 days.   During the 10 day intervening period between nestings (= “internesting interval”)  the turtle will continue to feed on jelly-like animals and data from other areas suggest that she may feed primarily at night (Eckert et al. 1986, 1989).  Such behavior is also quite unique for sea turtles as most other species do not feed during the nesting season and become quite sedentary.

The beaches of Trinidad support the second largest such nesting colony for the species in Western Hemisphere with one estimate of 500 - 900 nesting per year (Nathai-Gyan et al. 1987). This estimate is probably low as during peak nesting season 60 turtles have been recorded nesting per night at Matura Beach and 100 or more at Grande Riviere, however data collection to date has not been rigorous enough to determine actual numbers.  These are only two of the high density beaches on Trinidad with others along the north and east coasts (Fishing Pond, Paria Bay, Murphy

Bay, Petite and Gran Tacarib,

Madamas, Cachipa, Manzanillo, and Mayaro) probably sustaining equivalent numbers of turtles (Figure 3).  There is also some nesting on south coast at Guayaguayare, and Moruga and on the Caribbean coast of Tobago.  One minimum count of nesting activity recorded 3,523 nests on Fishing Pond and Matura beaches in 1994 which would be equivalent to approxi-

Figure 3 - Leatherback sea turtle nesting areas on the island of Trinidad.

mately 629 turtles on these beaches alone using the average of 5.6 nests per turtle per season that has been measured elsewhere in the Caribbean (Tucker and Frazer, 1994).  The nesting season for Trinidad and Tobago begins in early March, though nesting has been documented in February.  Based on research on the Caribbean island of St. Croix  where tropical barnacle colonization rates were used to indicate the turtles entrance into warmer waters, it was found that they begin nesting almost immediately upon entering the Caribbean (Eckert and Eckert, 1988).  After nesting, satellite telemetry data indicate that the turtles leave the Caribbean and disperse to the North Atlantic (Eckert, 1998)(Figure 4).  Such data demonstrates that Trinidad acts as a primary production area for the entire Atlantic Ocean population.

Global status of the leatherback sea turtle is Endangered as classified by the International Union for Conservation of Nature and Natural Resources’ (IUCN) Red Data Book, where taxa so clas-

Figure 4 - Post-nesting movement of 3 leatherback sea turtles from the nesting colony at Matura Bay Beach, Trinidad as determined by satellite telemetry.  Duration of trackline is 1 year for 20884 and 20886 and 3 months for 20885.

sified are considered to be “in danger of extinction and whose survival is unlikely if the causal factors continue operating” (Groombridge 1982).  The species is also included in Appendix I of the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (CITES), which bans all international trade in listed species.  Trinidad law also provides complete protection for the leatherback under both the Conservation of Wildlife Act (as amended in 1963) and by the 1975 Protection of Turtles and Turtle Eggs Regulation.  Further, international protection agreements of which Trinidad  is a signatory includes the SPAW protocol under the Cartegena Convention of 1983, with prohibits the taking, possession, killing (including incidentally) and commercial trade.  Significantly it also prohibits the disturbance of species such as leatherbacks during periods of breeding, incubation, estivation or migration as well as other periods of biological stress.

Recently, leatherback population status has become a topic of even greater concern, as sur-

veys of the largest nesting colony of leatherbacks in the world  indicate that global populations  have been reduced more than 80% in the last 10 years (Sarti et al, 1996).  Much of this decline has likely been due to the killing of leatherbacks incidental to  gillnet and longline swordfish fisheries hundreds of kilometers distant to the nesting beaches (Eckert and Sarti, 1997).  The value of Trinidad’s nesting population is immeasurably high to the continued survival of this species.

## **Internesting movement patterns**

Internesting movement patterns of leatherbacks in Trinidadian waters have been defined at

Figure 5 - Internesting movement of 3 female leatherback sea turtles from the nesting colony at Matura Bay Beach in Trinidad as determined by satellite telemetry in 1995.

least in part by 2 previous studies.   The first study utilized satellite transmitters to monitor 3 leatherbacks during multiple internesting periods for each turtle (S. Eckert in prep).  In this study the turtles ranged as far south as Guatuaro Pt. on the north coast to the east of Matelot (Figure 5).     While the residence areas chosen for each turtle was often different between nestings, the majority of locations were within 30 km of the coast.    The second study relied on detecting VHF transmitters attached to  female leatherbacks from

shore based receivers.  The pattern of internesting residence areas was very similar to the satellite telemetry study, though the data less complete (Figure 6).  In this latter study, the turtles generally resided within 30 km of the coast and were detected off the north coast as well as south of the nesting beach at Matura.

Figure 6 - Internesting movement of 4 female leatherback sea turtles from the nesting colony at Matura Bay Beach in Trinidad as determined by VHF telemetry in 1996.

## **Hearing capacity of turtles**

Testudinates (turtles and tortoises) have been characterized as deaf because many species exhibit little overt response (starting, orienting, running away) to transient sounds in their environment.  However, they possess auditory organs, and the few species that have been examined can hear, even if their sensitivity is not great.  Sounds at moderate to high signal-to-noise ratios within their hearing bandwidth (100-2000 kHz) will be detected.  At close range, seismic survey noise certainly falls into this category.  Impulses from airguns used for geophysical surveys have estimated source levels of 216-232 dB re 1 : Pa-m, while arrays (up to 70 elements), produce (calculated) source levels of 242-259 dB re 1 : Pa-m at ranges of 6-10 m (Richardson et al. 1995, pp. 136-9).  At close range, these impulses have fast rise times and peak levels approaching 240 dB re 1 : Pa-m.  Similar impulses can cause hearing losses in terrestrial animals after short-term exposures, so it is legitimate to ask whether auditory damage might occur if sea turtles were exposed at close range, and, if so, what the consequences might be.  In addition, low frequency components of these impulses (30-300 Hz) can travel for tens to hundreds of kilometers underwater with significant signal to noise ratios (e.g., Bowles et al. 1994).  Behavioral responses are therefore possible at great ranges from a shooting seismic survey vessel.

## **Hearing and Sensitivity to Vibration**

Sound reception in turtles and tortoises occurs along a pathway homologous to the familiar mammalian auditory pathway, but with greater limitations in frequency range and absolute sensitivity.  In testudinates, sound enters the ear via the skin of the head (analogous to the mammalian tympanic membrane, with no external ear or auditory canal).  In terrestrial turtles and tortoises, there is a tympanum, a thin circle of skin like a drumhead over the ear.  In sea turtles, this structure does not exist - the skin over the ear is indistinguishable from that elsewhere on the head.  For convenience, this skin is referred to as the cutaneous plate (Wever 1978).  Sound passes through it and through a fat-filled subcutaneous layer that acts as a channel to the middle ear.   There it

encounters a rod of bone consisting of two segments that serves the same function as the malleus, incus, and stapes of the mammalian ear - it conducts sound into the inner ear.  The outer segment is the extracolumella, a flattened, tough bone that abuts the subcutaneous layer and passes through a small, fluidfilled cavity homologous to the

mammalian middle ear.  The inner segment is the columella, a rod that runs through a channel in the quadrate bone to reach the otic cavity (Figure 7).   This rod is connected to the saccule (an organ homologous to the mammalian vestibular system) and pericapsular membrane of the inner ear by tough strands of tissue.  When the col-

Figure 7 - Diagram of the auditory mechanisms for the green sea turtle ( _Chelonia mydas_ ) (from Wever, 1978).

umella vibrates in response to sound, both the saccule and fluids of the inner ear vibrate as well.

In terrestrial animals, the bones of the middle ear match the impedance of a low-density medium (the air) to a high density medium (the fluids of the inner ear).  In testudinates, the matching is poorer, making sound transmission via the specialized structures of the outer and middle ear less efficient, and increasing the importance of sound conduction through other tissues into the inner ear (commonly called > bone conduction = ).  This is thought to explain the relative insensitivity of testudinates in air.  Underwater, where the impedance mismatch between the external medium and the animal’s tissues is small, differences between the two pathways are potentially small as well.  However, experiments with both airborne sound sources and vibrating rods held against the tissue have shown that testudinates achieve their best sensitivity when sound enters via the specialized structures of the auditory pathway (Ridgway et al. 1969), and that their sensitivity is considerably reduced after sectioning the of columella (Patterson and Gulick 1966) or removing the tympanum (Fay 1988).

Studies that measure hearing sensitivity using positive or negative reinforcement techniques (‘behavioral measures’) are widely regarded as the most sensitive and accurate measures of absolute hearing threshold.  Although reptiles are quite capable of learning, especially when the desired responses are species-typical behaviors elicited by food or noxious stimuli, their performance tends to be slow and unreliable, making behavioral tests prohibitively time-consuming (Suboski 1992).  Only one study has measured the hearing of any species of testudinate using a behavioral measure (most likely _Pseudemys scripta_ ; Patterson 1966, Patterson and Gulick 1966). Even if the effort required were not prohibitive, this method would be impractical for the leatherback sea turtle, as this endangered species has never been kept successfully in captivity.

Patterson’s turtles heard in the band between 40 and 1000 Hz, with best sensitivities of 45-50 dB SPL in the range from 200-700 Hz.   Sensitivity declined rapidly above 800 Hz and below 100 Hz.  Patterson also measured thresholds for detection of acceleration (vibration) on the carapace.  Sensitivity to vibration was fairly level from 20 to 640 Hz, ranging from -10 to 0 dB re 1 in/ s[2] , rolling off steeply above 640 Hz.  Patterson cut the columella and found no decrease in vibration sensitivity, but substantial hearing loss above 200 Hz.  He therefore concluded that low-frequency auditory sensitivity was replaced by vibration sensitivity below 64 Hz.

Other investigators have examined testudinate hearing using electrophysiological techniques, either by implanting electrodes in the cochlea, VIIIth nerve, or auditory brainstem, or by using brainstem auditory evoked responses recorded from the surface of the skull.  Wever and his coworkers measured the hearing of several species using cochlear potentials ( _Pseudemys scripta_ , _Chrysemis picta_ , _Clemmys insculpta_ , _Testudo graeca_ , and _Terrapine carolina_ ), showing good sensitivity in the range from 100-700 Hz.  These studies supported Patterson’s contention that the cochlea is the site of auditory perception.  However, electrophysiological measurements underestimated sensitivity in the best range and overestimated sensitivity at high frequencies relative to the behavioral measurements (Wever and Vernon 1956a, b, Patterson 1966, Wever 1978).  Bowles et al.

(1997) found that desert tortoises _(Gopherus agassizii_ ) were most sensitive in the range from 250-750 Hz using auditory-evoked potentials (AEPs).

The hearing of one species of sea turtle, the green sea turtle ( _Chelonia mydas_ ), has been examined in air using cochlear potentials (Ridgway et al. 1969, Wever 1978).  Their hearing resembled that of  terrestrial turtles, despite the large difference in size and absence of a specialized tympanum.  Best frequencies ranged from 150-700 Hz and were somewhat flattened at the high frequency end of the range (1000 to 2000 Hz) relative to Patterson’s results.  Ridgway et al. did not report estimates of the best sensitivities of the two turtles they tested - instead, they measured the sound pressure level required to produce a cochlear potential of 0.1 : V.  The greatest sensitivities they reported were  39 and 53 dB re 20 : Pa (65 and 79 dB re 1 : Pa), respectively, at 300-400 Hz.

Patterson’s turtles were tested at room temperature (~ 22 `E` C).  The best sensitivity of the most sensitive animal in his study was 37 dB re 20 : Pa (63 dB re 1 : Pa; Fay 1988).  However, this may not reflect the best performance possible.   The hearing of reptiles, including testudinates, is sensitive to changes in temperature.  Wever (1978) measured cochlear potentials of a specimen of the wood turtle ( _Clemmys insculpta_ ) over a 20 `E` C range.  The turtle’s electrophysiological response increased 5-fold in this range, but the increase was not monotonic.  Response increased slowly from 8-15 `E` C, rapidly from 15-20 `E` C, and reached an asymptote from 20-30 `E` C (Wever 1978). Bowles et al. (1997) estimated thresholds of the desert tortoise using AEPs.  The most sensitive of = 14 individuals was found to have a best sensitivity of 24 dB (at 250 Hz) in the species preferred temperature range (29-32 `E` C).  These results suggest that air and water temperature must be considered when measuring the sensitivity of marine turtles as well.

The literature on noise-induced hearing loss in reptiles is vanishingly small.  What is available suggests that reptiles may be somewhat more susceptible to temporary threshold shift (TTS) resulting from impulse noise exposure than might be expected based on their relative insensitivity. Susceptibility to permanent threshold shift (PTS) has not as yet been examined.  Brattstrom and Bondello (1983) exposed Mohave fringe-toed lizards ( _Uma scoparia_ ) to 500 s of taped dune buggy

noise at 100 dB (flat-weighted SPL; integration method not specified), with most of the energy below 1000 Hz.  Sensitivities were determined using AEPs measured from implanted electrodes in the right telencephalon.  Click-evoked responses showed a decrease in amplitude and an increase in latency relative to control conditions, but the magnitude of the threshold shift was not estimated.  Changes were detected within a few minutes of (i.e., in the time it took to complete tests with the click stimulus).  Bondello (1976) also exposed desert iguanas ( _Dipsosaurus dorsalis_ ) to shaped white noise at levels of 115 dB (Aweighted SPL) for 1 and 10 hr, showing a decrease in the amplitude of cochlear potentials that recovered within 4 weeks of the test exposure.  In this case, the sound was a poor model for seismic survey impulses.

Bowles et al. (1997) exposed desert tortoises to single and repeated simulated sonic booms, which shared with seismic survey impulses two important properties - most of the energy in the impulse lies at low frequency (~10 Hz vs. ~25 Hz for seismic survey impulses) and the rise time of the impulse is very rapid (400 : s in the Bowles et al. study and 1-1.5 ms for seismic survey impulses).  None of the 8 test tortoises experienced TTS after exposure to single or paired sonic booms (143 dB peak flat SPL), but exposure to a sequence of 10 booms separated by 3 s produced detectable TTS in half of the tortoises (the most sensitive individual experienced 30 dB of temporary loss).   Shifts were estimated within 15 min of exposure; all except one recovered completely within 2 hr (the remaining tortoise had recovered its hearing within 48 hr).

## **Behavioral Responses of Reptiles to Noise and Vibration**

Early  observations of testudinate behavior in response to sounds led naturalists to believe they were deaf (Patterson 1966, Carr 1952, Pope 1939).  However, negative reinforcement techniques showed that _Chrysemys_ (probably _C. picta_ ) could hear whistles and bell tones (Andrews 1915) and _Emys orbicularis_ could hear pipe organ and bell tones (Poliakov 1930), although responses were not elicited very reliably (Andrews 1915, Kuroda 1923).  Several investigators reported that turtles exhibit an > electro-defensive reflex = (startle) to vibration, but not to purely acoustic stimuli (ringing bells, high frequency tones; Chernomordikov 1958, Karimova 1958).  These observations

supported the hypothesis that testudinates could hear, but did not have an acoustically-stimulated startle reflex.

Species-typical defensive responses of testudinates to the approach of danger include alerting, starting, running, diving, urinating, freezing, and withdrawing into the shell.  It is not known what part of this repertoire is elicited by acoustic transients with fast rise times, although a handful of accounts indicate that freezing is a common response of reptiles and anurans (Wever and Vernon 1960, Suboski 1992, Bowles et al. 1997).  Freezing is an abrupt cessation of motion that persists from a few seconds to hours.  The more intense the stimulus, the more profound and protracted the inactivity.  Frogs will allow themselves to be shocked to death as increasing stimulus levels trigger greater and greater inactivity (McGill 1960).  Most lizards exposed to shock cease to respond with successive exposures, even when trained, lapsing into immobility as noxious stimuli are repeated (a few species can learn to escape reliably if provided an appropriate escape route or are given species-appropriate noxious stimuli; Suboski 1992).  Terrestrial testudinates are very consistent in their response - they drop, freeze, and (if approached or touched) withdraw into their shells (Ellis and Spigel 1966, Granada et al. 1965, Farris and Breuning 1977).  Responses of aquatic forms have not been reported.

For sea turtles underwater, freezing seems likely to have maladaptive consequences because, unlike their terrestrial counterparts, sea turtles are only lightly armored and incapable of retracting their limbs.  Freezing would thus expose them to greater predation risk than fleeing or hiding.   This is particularly true for the leatherback with its fragile dermis.   However, there is very limited data to describe the behavioral responses of sea turtles to any kind of sound.  Lenhardt (1994) exposed loggerhead sea turtles ( _Caretta caretta_ ) to underwater vibration in the range from 20-80 Hz using an accelerometer coupled to the walls of the test pool and found that turtles swam abruptly to the surface in response to the exposures at > high levels = (not quantified).  O’Hara and Wilcox (1989) exposed loggerhead sea turtles ( _Caretta caretta_ ) to low-frequency impulses from a seismic survey airgun in a 300 x 45 m pen.  The absolute levels of the impulses from these stimuli were not

measured at the point of reception, but were characterized as having peak levels of 220-230 dB re 1 `F` Pa (at 1 m) at most and were fired at rates of  8/min or higher during the experiment.  Loggerhead turtles rested in the net that held the sound sources regardless of the impulses, but came within 30 m of the active sources significantly less often when they were swimming.  In some cases, the turtles swam away from the source, but others dropped to the bottom.  Since the investigators did not quantify the sound field within the test pen or observe details of the turtle’s responses, it is unclear whether the turtles dropped to the bottom because they froze or because they had found an area where impulse level was more moderate (close to a reflecting surface).

Anecdotal accounts also suggest that sea turtles respond behaviorally to meaningful continuous noise, such as the sound of an approaching vessel, with avoidance.  In an unpublished study (Eckert pers. obs.) leatherback turtles tracked by a 65' vessel showed avoidance behavior of the vessel at approximately 2-3 km distance.  Avoidance was characterized by abrupt change in swimming direction and a change in submergence patterns.

Based on available information, the plausible potentially-damaging behaviors of turtles in response to seismic survey impulses are (1) significant changes in normal behavior patterns, (2) increased energetic expenditures resulting from avoidance, (4) inappropriate behavioral responses (fleeing or extended surface periods), and (5) failure to respond to biologically-important signals due to noise masking or attentional difficulties.  In order for any of these responses to be damaging, turtles would have to be exposed over long periods.

## **Importance of auditory sensitivity**

While hearing sensitivity has not been measured for the leatherback sea turtle, it plays an important role in other pelagic vertebrates as a means to gather information in an environment where vision is effective only at short range.  In the leatherback, passive reception of acoustic signals may play an important role in avoiding danger (e.g. identifying the calls of hunting killer whales - a predator on leatherback turtles while in the tropics, Caldwell and Caldwell, 1969), longrange navigation, or identification of nesting beaches (Lenhardt, et al. 1983).

## **Methods**

This research program was subdivided into 2 categories.  Those experiments which investigate behavioral responses to the airgun survey (1) and (2) those which investigate hearing sensitivity.  Because many of the techniques required for such work are experimental on the leatherback, and the survey schedule was very limited, the project was designed as a preliminary research program to investigate the feasibility of such research on this species, and gather as much information on leatherback hearing sensitivity and behavioral responses to airgun surveys as possible.

## **Monitoring Turtle Movements and Behavior.**

High resolution data on turtle movements is important in understanding behavioral responses to airgun generated noise.  For this study turtles were to carry a combination of instruments that monitor location and dive patterns (Figure 8).   Instrument arrays were mounted to a

Figure 8.  Instrument pack with TDR, VHF transmitter and UVR.

plastic plate and attached to a harness which is placed on the turtle while she is nesting (Eckert and Eckert, 1986, Eckert et al. 1996).  A description of the instruments follows:

GPS Tracker - This prototype instrument was to be used for the first time on this project.  It consists of a Garmin Global Positioning System receiver (GPS), linked to a 5 watt Yaesu transceiver and a pressure switch (Figure 9).  The GPS and the transceiver are controlled by a  custom designed interface.   Upon surfacing the GPS is powered up and a location is collected.  The location is then transmitted to a shore base and logged on the base computer.  Bench tests of the system indicated that a high level of performance could be anticipated with such system with 80% of leatherback s u r f a c i n g s

long enough to establish a GPS location and transmit

Figure 9.  Nesting leatherback sea turtle with prototype GPS transmitter.

that data to shore.  Expected  range of the system was 25 miles.  Further enhancement to range was available by utilizing a radio relay  elevated on a tower, or by suspending the relay from  a parasail kite.

As a backup for tracking turtles offshore and to enhance detection of turtles on the nesting beach each turtle was equipped with a VHF transmitter. Location of a turtle was estimated by determining its compass bearing from two different reception points

Figure 10.  VHF tracking station.

using radio receivers (Telonics TR-4) with 5 element YAGI (directional) antennas (Figure 10).  Error of the quality of the bearings was determined by placing a transmitter at a known  location and determining that location from different  reception points.  This same technique was also used to determine maximum reception distance of the system.

Time Depth Recorder (TDR) - This small electronic microprocessor (Wildlife Computer  Mk5) records dive depth, dive duration, surface time, and calculates bottom duration, ascent and descent rates.  Depth resolution is to 2 meters. The data is logged at programmed intervals (in this experiment, every 20 seconds) for later retrieval and downloading to computer. Such an instrument provides an important perspective on the submerged behavior of the turtle.

Velocity/Distance Recorder (UVR) - This electronic counter (Ultramarine instruments), utilizes a small turbine to integrate revolutions of the turbine over time to indicate speed as well as measure distance traveled.  Data is stored in the instruments memory for downloading after recovery.

## **Measurement of Background Noise Levels**

Background noise levels were collected to determine the influence of ambient noise on the hearing tests.  At both study sites (Matura and Grand Riviere Beaches), there was a steeply sloped forebeach and a flat hindbeach.  On the forebeach, female leatherback sea turtles were exposed to surf noise coming directly from the line of breakers offshore (within 100 m), as well as reflected noise from the forebeach.  On the hindbeach, noise was attenuated considerably by distance, reflected away by the forebeach, and absorbed by sand.  Sand piled by the digging female also attenuated noise.

One hour samples of ambient noise were collected with a Larson-Davis 820 community noise monitor (LD820) deployed on the crest of the beach and ~30 m inland on the hindbeach. Deployments were made on nights with little wind (< 5 kt) and with substantial wind (10-15 kt).

Noise was also recorded on a Tascam DAT.  In both cases, data were collected through a 2@ ACO 7013 instrumentation microphone fitted with a 15 cm open-pore foam wind-ball to eliminate wind noise (<15 kt = wind speed), and mounted on a pole at the height of a leatherback sea turtle s head (15 cm).  The microphone faced the line of surf.  Hourly C-weighted equivalent sound levels (L eq[) and spectra were obtained] (C-weighting was used to remove wind noise).

## **Measurements of Hearing Threshold Using Auditory-Evoked Potentials**

Far-field auditory-evoked potentials (AEPs) are electrical potentials generated by groups of neurons in the cochlea, VIIIth nerve, or brain when the ear is stimulated by sound.  Far-field AEPs are measured by placing electrodes close to populations of neurons, rather than  implanted within nerve cells.  Far-field AEPs are used in clinical settings to measure electrophysiological responses of humans and protected animals because they pose no danger to the test subject.  AEPs generated in the auditory brainstem are called auditory brainstem responses (ABRs).  These are used to evaluate hearing because they are relatively insensitive to subject state and small variations in electrode placement, are strongly correlated with changes in stimulus frequency and amplitude, can be used to determine threshold at many frequencies in a short time, and occur in a wide variety of animals.  They appear at medium latencies, typically 5-20 ms after exposure to a stimulus, following short-latency AEPs like the cochlear microphonic.

In order for an AEP to be detectable, there must be a high degree of synchrony in the firing of populations of neurons and the resulting signal must conduct well through the surrounding tissues.  These criteria may be met by activity of a number of structures within the ear and brain, ranging from the VIIIth nerve to the midbrain.  In animals whose neurophysiology is poorly understood, such as the leatherback, it will not always be obvious where an evoked response is generated. Click-evoked ABRs and other AEPs have been elicited from reptiles in previous studies (Corwin et al. 1982, Bullock 1985).

Stimuli eliciting  AEPs may be clicks, used to measure broadband hearing sensitivity; shaped tone-bursts, used to measure frequency-specific sensitivity; or more complex waveforms.  The potentials elicited by these signals are measured as voltage differences between electrodes inserted on either side of the structure of interest.  For this study, activity in the cochlea, VIIIth nerve and brainstem were of interest. Because these structures are in close proximity in the leatherback sea turtle, all were likely to contribute to any AEP measured.

AEPs collected following a single stimulus presentation appear to have a random waveform. However, by collecting samples in synchrony with test stimulus presentations, then averaging many samples, activity unrelated to test stimuli is eliminated.  Individual variability in the resulting AEP waveform is high, but a characteristic series of peaks  can be identified after examining a number of individuals of each species.  The number of averages used to generate an AEP waveform is selected to maximize waveform amplitude while minimizing measurement time.

AEP waveform peaks are generated as populations of neurons in the brainstem discharge simultaneously.  As the intensity of a test stimulus decreases, amplitude of the AEPs decreases as well.  At low stimulus amplitudes, these peaks are no longer detectable against the background of electrophysiological and electrical noise in the measurement system.  The least detectable waveform is therefore an estimate of animal threshold.  Also, as stimulus level decreases, latency from the stimulus onset to each peak increases (at least in ABRs).  Changing latencies are also an indication of decreasing sensitivity.

While ABR waveforms have been characterized in great detail for humans and laboratory animals, relatively little is known about similar electrical activity in non-mammalian vertebrates.  The only systematic measurements of far-field, whole brain potentials from testudinates were collected by Bullock and his coworkers (Corwin et al. 1982, Bullock 1985) from 3 red-eared turtles ( _Pseudemys scripta elegans;_ Figure 6).  These investigators showed that both ABRs and frequency-following responses (AEPs that follow the time-varying pressure of the input signal precisely) can be elicited from turtles, but did not attempt to obtain measurements of threshold.

Cochlear potentials, collected by placing electrodes within the otic capsule, were collected by Ridgway et al. (1969) to measure the relative sensitivity of two green sea turtles at frequencies between 40 and 2000 Hz.  Although Ridgway _et al._ did not report absolute sensitivities, there is sufficient data in their paper to show that the turtles could hear down to at least 65 and 78 dB re 1 `F` Pa in air (=39 and 42 dB re 20 `F` Pa, respectively).  Ridgway _et al_ . did not measure the least-detectable waveform; rather, they used the stimulus level required to produce a 0.1 `F` V potential.  Therefore, it is possible that greater sensitivity could have been detected.  The two turtles were most sensitive at 200-500 Hz, consistent with measurements made from other testudinates.

Generally speaking, if a detectable AEP is found, the subject animal can hear the test stimuli. However, if no AEP is detected, the response may simply lack sufficient signal level to be detected above considerable electrophysiological and electrical ambient noise.  Potentials from skeletal muscles and the heart are particularly likely to contaminate measurements.  In addition, when the brainstem is small and deeply embedded within the head, as is the case for sea turtles, proper electrode placement can be difficult.  Electrodes must be placed within 1-2 cm of the active neurons in obtain an adequate waveform.

In mammals, the least detectable ABR typically yields a somewhat higher, _i.e._ , less sensitive, estimate of threshold than conditioned responses (behavioral measures).  Under optimal conditions, the difference may be as little as 5 dB.  For animals that are difficult to condition, such as reptiles, it is unclear which method will yield the best estimate of threshold.  As yet, no experiments comparing the two methods have been conducted in any reptile.

The present experiments were designed to elicit ABR waveforms at specific frequencies in order to obtain an estimate of the leatherback = s auditory threshold function.  Tone pips used to stimulate ABR waveforms are only a few milliseconds in duration and are shaped at onset and offset.  In theory, shaping narrows the signal in the frequency domain while still stimulating a good ABR; in practice, broader-band clicks consisting of a single cycle of a pure tone are often needed to elicit appropriate responses.  At very low frequencies, the tone pip must be of relatively long duration, but long waveforms are often ineffective at eliciting ABRs and the resulting waveform is subject to distortion as

frequency-following responses begin to overlap.  Stimuli at frequencies below about 500 Hz are not normally collected for clinical applications because of this.  However, because turtle hearing is maximally sensitive at low frequencies (250-500 Hz), both 250 and 500 Hz signals were tested during the present experiments.  In the event that frequency-following AEP = s were detected instead of ABR = s, these would be used as an indication of hearing ability.

## **Measuring Evoked Response Waveforms of Leatherback Sea Turtles**

Adult female leatherback sea turtles become relatively quiescent while laying eggs, tolerating human approach and some manipulation.  Leatherback sea turtle females can thus be instrumented  for evoked response measurements during the laying phase of nesting.

Surface electrodes could not be used, as the cochlea, VIIth nerve, and auditory brainstem lies  more than 2 cm centimeters from the skin surface within the bony case of the skull in this species (Bowles and Eckert, pers obs).  To select the insertion site, the heads of similarly-sized leatherbacks that had been salvaged from a stranding along the Atlantic coast of Georgia were dissected.  The site was free of large blood vessels (the large dorsal sinus is distal to this location on either side of the neck), and lay between two large retractor muscles in the neck of the turtle.  The depth of major structures that could guide electrode placement were identified, including the rear margin of the skull, the occipital condyles, and the atlas of the first cervical vertebra.

Electrodes were made with 15-cm lengths of hair-fine, flexible, insulated laryngeal electrode wire (0.0001 mm enameled alloy C wire, Jelliff Manufacturing Co.) wound together = and stripped of insulation within 5 mm of the tip.  Electrodes were hooked over the tip of a 3.5 20-gauge spinal tap needle for insertion(Figure 11).

Figure 11.  Sound stimuli were projected through calibrated TDH 39D headphones (flat to 8.5 kHz) placed over the cuticular plate on both sides of the turtle’s head.

After considerable experimentation with placements near the brainstem and cochlea, the active and reference electrodes were placed on either side of the brainstem, immediately anterior to the first vertebra against the occipital condyles.  A ground electrode was placed 2.5 cm under the skin below the forward peak of the carapace, in fatty connective tissue.

Before electrode placement, the insertion site was swabbed carefully with alcohol and Betadine  to minimize risk of infection. Injectable lidocaine Hcl (1%) was injected subcutaneously to desensitize the skin and elec-

trode placement was completed as quickly as possible to minimize discomfort.  The turtles were not sedated or restrained, yet they rarely responded  to electrode placement.  Females that exhibited any response to the procedure were not used as subjects.  AEP measurements began as soon as the electrodes were placed and were terminated when muscle potentials became prohibitively frequent or when the turtle left the nest.  As the turtle began to move, the hair-fine and flexible electrodes were simply pulled free.

Stimuli were projected through calibrated  TDH 39D headphones (flat to 8.5 kHz) = placed over the cuticular plate on both sides of the turtle s head.  The site was chosen by feeling for the pad of fatty tissue underneath.

Stimuli were produced by a BioLogic Traveller III system.  Levels were calibrated during preliminary measurements using a 2@ ACO 7013 instrumentation microphone connected to a calibrated measurement system and placed under the earpiece of the headphone (Figure 12).

Normally, when AEP measurements are collected, animals (and often children as well) are sedated or anaesthetized to reduce muscle movement.  However, an effort involving sedation or anaesthesia was outside the scope of the present feasibility study.

Figure 12.  Hearing tests were conducted during the quiescent period while the turtle was egg laying.

Turtles were equipped with electrodes during the final stages of nest digging.  AEP measurements were made during egg-laying and for as long as possible while the turtle was filling the nest. Under good conditions, 15-20 minutes of data could be obtained.  Given the large number of averages necessary to obtain a single waveform, this period proved unacceptably short.  A maximum of 10 acceptable waveform averages could be collected from each turtle, yielding only ~5 usable measurements (2-3 replicates had to be collected at each frequency/level combination).  It was impossible to collect enough data to estimate threshold at more than one frequency for any given turtle.

Electrode impedance was kept less than 10 k S and inter-electrode impedance less than 5 k S .  Initial measurements at high test signal levels (tone pips at 80 or 90 dB SPL [RMS level]) were collected to insure that an AEP was detectable.  Then the stimulus level was dropped in large steps (20 dB decrements) to obtain an approximate estimate of threshold as quickly as possible.  If time permitted, intermediate-level measurements were collected around the estimated threshold thereafter.

The stimuli were pure tone pips at 250, 500 and 1000 Hz.  Each tone pip was shaped, consisting of a rising, steady state, and declining portion.  Shaping was used to insure that the stimulus had a very narrow bandwidth.

Stimuli were presented at a rate of 29/s.  The amplified electrophysiological signal from the electrodes was high-pass filtered at 100 and low-pass filtered at 3000 Hz.  Potentials were collected for 30 ms after stimulus presentation.  System signal gain was set as high as possible and many stimulus presentations were averaged to determine whether an AER waveform was present (1024 to >6000 averages per waveform).  The averaged waveform was monitored by the system operator in real time, and averaging was discontinued when the AEP waveform ceased to change.  At least two replicate waveforms were collected except when the AEP waveform was very obvious.  Waveforms were saved on disk for further analysis.

All threshold estimates were made by one experienced analyst (A. Bowles).  A detectable evoked response was one in which replicates were closely matched at the highest peak of the waveform and the waveform was visibly greater than the surrounding electrical ambient.

Because all experiments were collected on the beach from exercising turtles, internal temperature was likely to vary considerably from individual to individual.  Cloacal temperatures were collected from each individual as an estimate of cochlear temperature.

## **Results**

## **Movement patterns**

Leatherback #1 (Figure 13)

Delays by the equipment designer/manufacturer meant that the GPS tracking instruments would not arrive and be ready for deployment until June, so we deployed one VHF transmitter on a 163 cm (over-the-curve) turtle at 23:30 h on 30 May at Matura Beach to initiate a movement study.  Tests of the VHF tracking system revealed that the transmitters had an accurate reception range of 25 km (surface to surface) and an average accuracy of 5 `E` .  Thus, all single bearings are expressed as triangular regions 25 km long with a 10 `E` spread.  Where such regions intersect the location is expressed as a polygon.

Upon leaving the beach, leatherback  #1, swam directly offshore and by morning was

Figure 13 - Internesting locations as detected by VHF telemetry for a 163 cm long female leatherback sea turtle (Leatherback #1).

detected moving north toward Toco Point.   Between 1301h and 1345h  it was located 12.5 km from Matura Beach and approximately 2.5 km from shore.   Between 1423h and 1808h it was in the area just to the south of Toco Point, again relatively close to shore.  Despite regular efforts to find the turtle, it was not detected again until 3 June when it was found 8 km  northeast of  the town of Matelot.  While it is impossible to know where the turtle resided during the intervening days it is likely that it had either moved off the north coast in excess of 25 km or possibly along the coast more than 25 km west of Matelot (where the north coast road ends).  Given the propensity for this turtle to remain near the coast, the latter location is more likely.  On 4 June between 1325 h and 1635h, the turtle was detected about 2 km directly north of Toco Point and it remained in this area through 7 June.  On 8 June the turtle began to move south from Toco Point and by early morning (0118 h) of 9 June was directly east of Balandra Bay (though the exact distance is unknown). Over the next 23 hours she moved north back near Toco Point, and then south again to the nesting beach at Matura.  She nested at  2312 h on Matura Beach, and the transmitter was recovered.

## Leatherback #2

The GPS tracking instruments continued to be problematic with numerous electronic and battery failures.  We repeatedly sent them back to the manufacturer for repair and finally by mid-June we had what we believed to be one working GPS tracking instrument.  This GPS was deployed on a 159 cm  (carapace over-the-curve)  turtle on June 12 at 2115h with a full instrument array, including a velocity/distance meter, time-depth-recorder and VHF transmitter.  Upon departure the turtle swam directly offshore, and the GPS tracking instrument appeared to be functioning properly.  Within 6 hours, however the turtle was no longer detectable by VHF or GPS and based on the bearing of departure the turtle appears to have left Trinidad.  Despite continuous monitoring for the next 3 weeks, this turtle was not detected again.

## Leatherback #3 (Figure 14)

Having already deployed the only functioning GPS instrument, we then deployed the final instrument array with a VHF radio transmitter, a velocity/distance recorder and a time-depth-recorder on a 158 cm leatherback at 2300 h on 12 June at Matura Beach.   The next day  at 1425 h the turtle was detected directly south of Toco Pt. and approximately 10 km from shore.  On 14 June the turtle appeared to have remained in the same area.   On 15 June, the turtle’s location was determined to be directly east of Balandra Bay, and given how close to shore it had been the previous 2 days, was also likely within 10 km.  This turtle was not detected on 16 June, however by 17 June it was determined to be south of Balandra Bay and within a few km of the coast.  On 18 June good triangulation determined that the turtle was residing east-southeast of Balandra Bay within 6 km of shore and it remained in this location from at least 1000 h - 1645 h.  By 19 June it appears that leatherback # 3 had moved farther offshore (out of reception range) but it was undetected again despite regular searching.  Leatherback #3 returned to nest at Fishing Pond beach on 22 June at 20:49 hours.  The instrument array was recovered by the Fishing Pond sea turtle patrol.

## Dive Profiles

Leatherback # 3 was the only turtle equipped with a dive recorder that was recovered (Figure 15).   An examination of the dive profiles can provide a good perspective on the turtle’s activities during the 10 day internesting interval.  Upon leaving the nesting beach dives approached the bottom with the turtle gradually making deeper dives as she  moved offshore.  By 0800 on the morning of the 13th the turtle settled into a routine pattern of daytime dives between 18 and 28 m, and night dives shallower than 18m.  This dive depth pattern continued through 14 June until dusk at about 1900 h when the dives remained shallow near 18 m.  Dive depths continued to be shallow until dawn at 0600 h, when they gradually deepened to 28 m at approx. 1000 h. Subsequent dive depths were progressively shallower until 1900 h when they were approximately 10 m.  This daily pattern continued until June 19 when the maximum dive depths increased to 44 m, which suggests that the turtle may have moved to deeper water.  On June 20 and 21 all diving was distinctly shallow and it is clear that the turtle had modified its diving pattern.

## Dive Depths

Mean dive depth was 12.8 meters, however this value is somewhat misleading as a frequency distribution of dive depth is heavily skewed to the left (Figure 16).  Dive depths between 1 and 3 meters in depth were most common (= modal depth).  Excluding dives less than 5 meters as representing primarily surfacing behavior, the dive depths are trimodal with dives between 5-7 meters, 15 - 16 meters and 23 - 25 meters.  The maximum dive depth was 43 meters as might be expected given the shallow water surrounding Trinidad.

## Dive Durations

Dive durations averaged 4.1 minutes, with the maximum duration of 17 minutes (Figure 16). Dive durations are bimodal with dives between 0  and 1 minute and 4 - 6 minutes.

## Surface Interval

The surface interval (time spent on surface between dives) was generally very short

Figure 16 - Summary frequency distributions of dive data from a 158cm female leatherback sea turtle, during one internesting interval, Trinidad.

with a mean of 1.27 minutes (Figure 16).  The far majority of surfacing were 1 minute or less.  Maximum surface interval was 39 minutes.

## Bottom Interval

The bottom interval (time spent at maximum depth before returning to the surface) averaged 2.043 minutes, with the modal  frequency less than 1 minute (Figure 16).

## Ascent and Descent Rates

The average descent rate was faster (.226 m/s) than the average ascent rate (.199 m/ s)(Figure 16).  However, this statistic may be somewhat misleading because the data for both descent and ascent rates are skewed.  Modal  rates are probably better representatives of typical behavior.  Modal descent rate is actually slower (.1 - .3 m/s) than modal ascent rates (.2 - .4 m/s).

## Correlations:

Dive depth and dive duration are strongly and positively correlated (r = .84405, Figure 17) indicating that swim speeds are relatively constant throughout the dives.   Post-dive surface intervals and dive times,

however are not correlated r =

.08071, Figure 18).  This indicates that the turtle required little or no surface rest between dives, which also explains why surface intervals are typically short.  Such information suggests that the turtle was not exceeding

normal aerobic capacity during its dives.

## Swim Speed

There were no results from the swim speed recorder, due to sand fouling when the turtle left the nesting beach. While such fouling is uncommon because the turbine intake opening is screened, sea conditions were exceptionally rough this year which caused an in-

crease in surf activity and water turbidity.  The high quantity of particulate in the water defeated the intake screening and  fouled the turbine.

## Comparison of Dive Patterns and Turtle Location

The regular  pattern of dive depths seem to suggest that the turtle was residing in similar habitats and water depths during the first half of the  internesting interval. This data is well confirmed by the locations established by VHF tracking, which placed the turtle close to the coast between the nesting beach and Toco Point for the duration.  The change in dive depths which occurred on June 19 is consistent with the turtle’s location, which had moved offshore.  It is unfortunate that the turtle was undetectable after the 19th, but based on dive depths it is likely that the turtle had moved back near shore as it approached the nesting beach.

## Comparison of Movement Patterns to Other Studies.

In the 2 other studies of the internesting movements of leatherback sea turtles nesting at Matura Beach a pattern emerges that leatherbacks nesting at Matura will range  as far south as Point Guatuaro and around Toco Point to the north coast of Trinidad as far west as Matelot.  The majority of the time was spent within 30 km of the coast and off the east coast, between Toco

Point and Manzanillo Point.  There is nothing to indicate that leatherback #1 or leatherback #2 from this season behaved in a manner inconsistent with the patterns observed in the previous 2 years.  Both of these turtles appear to have remained within the internesting habitats typical for leatherbacks from the Matura Beach nesting colony.

For the days in which locations were determined, the closest either turtle came to the seismic survey area was 44 km.  There is a possibility that leatherback #3 moved closer to the survey area between 19 - 22 July, because this was the turtle = s direction of movement when the signal was lost, however lack of location data on this turtle during this period make this difficult to confirm.

## Comparison of Dive Behavior with previous studies.

In 1995 we deployed a single TDR on a 150 cm female leatherback in a manner identical to this project, and the resulting data provides the only comparable data set for examining dive behavior of leatherbacks in Trinidad. (Figure19).  Qualitatively the dive patterns of the 2 turtles are similar.  Dives were frequent, appeared to follow bottom contours, had a tendency to be deeper during daylight hours.  Quantitatively there are differences between these 2 turtles with the turtle from 1997 diving for shorter durations, having shorter surface intervals, spending less time on the bottom and descending and ascending more quickly (Figure 20).    However it is not possible from this limited data to determine if the differences are due to these being different turtles,  between-year  variability, the seismic surveys or any other number of variables.  Diving studies on leatherbacks in other areas of the world, including St. Croix in the U.S. Virgin Islands and Malaysia demonstrate that the range of variation in dive behavior between individual turtles can be quite large (Eckert et al. 1996).

## Ambient Noise Measurements

Noise levels on the beach were high enough that hearing measurements were likely to

have been noise limited to some extent.  The major contributing sources were wind noise, surf noise and biotic sources in the nearby forest ( _e.g_ ., coqui frogs at Matura Beach).  Wind noise probably affected measurements to an unpredictable extent when wind speed was relatively high (10-15 kt).   When it was low, the hourly average level on the hindbeach was 52.8 dB (C-weighted equivalent continuous sound pressure level [L eq1h[]).   In the presence of heavy surf and windy gusts, the level was around 78] dB.

Headphones attenuated these noise sources by 15-20 dB, presuming that most noise was conducted to the turtle = s ear via the cuticular plate.  If turtles had demonstrated thresholds of ~30-50 dB, it is likely that they would have been masked by broadband noise.   In the range likely to have been heard well by the turtles, the spectrum of noise was fairly flat.

## Measurements of evoked potentials

A total of 32 turtles were instrumented (Table 1).  From these, 146 AEP waveform measurements were collected, averaging 4.7 per turtle (Table 2).  As expected, turtle movement during laying made measurements difficult to collect. Of the samples collected, 26 had a characteristic waveform (one that was similar from measurement to measurement) of short to medium latency (5-15 ms).

Electrode placements at a distance from the brainstem did not yield a detectable waveform.  Initially, this was thought to eliminate the possibility that the electrodes were measuring self noise from the Bio-Logic system or spurious potentials from elsewhere in the animal.

However, the AEP waveforms that were actually obtained did not conform to the criteria for an ABR (Corwin _et al._ 1982; see Figure 21).  Instead, they resembled the input stimulus, with no or very little latency shift relative to  stimulus onset (Figure 22).  At low intensities, the amplitude of the AER waveforms decreased, but there was still no latency shift.

In contrast, ABR and frequencyfollowing responses are known change their form and latency as stimuli decrease in level.  At 250 Hz, the waveform appeared phaseshifted, as though severe electrical interference had contaminated the signal.  These observations suggested that the waveform was a product, at least in part, of electrical cross-talk.

Figure 21 - Example of turtle auditory brainstem response to a 1 kHz click

Unfortunately, this proved to be the case - the same waveform detected in the vicin= ity of the turtles brains also appeared when there was no chance that an AEP could be detect= able, _e.g._ , with the electrodes placed on an experimenter s arm.   After systematically eliminating possible sources of interference and poor grounding, cross-talk between the projecting system (headphones, output amplifier) and receiving system (electrode, input amplifier) proved to be the source of the interfering signal.  This interference did not appear when ABR measurements, which have longer latencies, were collected using the BioLogic system (e.g., from desert tortoises).  However, no detectable ABRs were obtained from the leatherback sea turtles. Therefore, the present effort provided only two lines of evidence that an AEP had been obtained from the turtles:

(1) The waveform elicited by 500 Hz tone pips appeared only intermittently when the electrodes were placed away from the brain at equivalent separation.  When placed correctly, the waveform was obtained reliably.

(2) The averaged waveform collected using 250 Hz tone pips was distorted (Figure 23), suggesting that an endogenous signal from the turtle and a spurious signal from the BioLogic system were interfering (compare the waveform of the received > evoked potential = from Figure 23 with Figure 22).   A similar effect was uncovered during experiments with 1000 Hz tone pips. The electrical interference made it impossible to collect threshold measurements from the leatherback sea turtles.
